Abstract 
The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) enables advanced developments in automotive systems 
to communicate with interconnected devices, enhancing traffic flow, security, and util-
ity functions. Edge computing and Digital Twins (DTs) facilitate effective resource 
management in the IoV. DTs replicate real entities in the virtual domain with real-time 
control, diagnostics, maintenance, and better management. With edge computing, 
processing data near the source, these technologies significantly lower response time 
and optimize system performance. This study provides a comprehensive overview 
of the latest resource management strategies in DT-enabled edge computing for IoV. 
Existing approaches are then discussed and compared using clustering, matching, 
and offloading approaches. Clustering groups of vehicles and devices to manage 
resources while assigning resources by mapping demand and availability. Offload-
ing techniques delegate computation to edge servers, thereby controlling resources. 
The paper outlines the strengths and weaknesses of each method, as well as research 
directions, including the integration of artificial intelligence, security and privacy issues, 
and interoperability standards.

Introduction
Context
The Internet of Things (IoT) represents a global network connecting virtually every-
thing. This ecosystem comprises a variety of interconnected subsystems that cover vari-
ous applications [1]. Internet of Vehicles (IoV) is emerging as a specific IoT subsystem 
focusing on Internet-enabled vehicles as mobile units within the network [2]. The core 
concept of IoV revolves around the networking and collaborative interaction of vehicles 
and intelligent devices [3].
The IoV technology facilitates data generation, transmission, and processing, 
addressing critical challenges such as traffic congestion, travel times, pollution lev-
els, and accident rates. Aside from these basic attributes, the IoV also features play-
back and file-sharing capabilities [4]. Several factors must be considered, including

Problem statement
The rapid development of IoV signals an era of automotive technology revolution, where 
automobiles, infrastructure, and devices converge for optimal traffic control, safety, and 
user experience [6, 7]. The network platform supports real-time information exchange 
and automobile coordination, creating intelligent and efficient transportation networks 
[8]. Exponential growth is observed in connected automobiles, and the complexity of 
IoV applications is exceptionally high; therefore, effective resource management meth-
ods are required to ensure optimal reliability and performance [9]. Emerging next-gen-
eration technologies, such as Digital Twin (DT) technology and edge computing, are 
poised to address IoV resource management challenges, including real-time tracking, 
prognostic maintenance, and operational optimization [10, 11].
Motivation and contribution
Edge computing supports the DT technology by processing data at the network 
edge near its source. This reduces latency, ensures data security, and alleviates the 
cloud server burden [12]. Edge computing within the IoV entails placing computing 
resources in roadside and on-board units, paving the way for faster and more efficient 
data handling and increased resource availability [13].
Optimal management of resources is needed for the efficient deployment and 
execution of IoV systems. It involves assigning and scheduling computation, net-
work, and storage resources to handle the varying requirements of IoV applications 
[14]. Adequate resource management enables IoV systems to efficiently manage vast 
amounts of data and diverse application requirements, resulting in improved perfor-
mance, reduced latency, and an enhanced user experience. This research will provide 
a holistic review of existing resource management techniques for DT-enabled edge 
computing for IoV. Table 1 provides a list of abbreviations applied throughout this 
research. The specific research goals of this survey are as follows:
•	 Reviewing and classifying current resource management approaches: several 
methods and techniques applied to DT-enabled edge computing for IoV are dis-
cussed, with a focus on clustering, matching, and offloading approaches.
•	 Benefit and limitation analysis: each method is evaluated for its strengths and 
weaknesses to offer a balanced view of its application for various IoV applications.
•	 Future research directions and challenges: to advance the subject area, future

Internet of vehicles
The IoV model depicts a network architecture that utilizes data generated by networked 
vehicles. IoV technology offers interactivity with multiple Electronic Control Units 
(ECUs) and on-board sensors, with applications extending to autonomous driving, data 
dissemination, and multimedia services [15]. Additionally, IoV expands its areas of con-
cern to include communication among various entities on the road, augmenting the 
on-board experience, enhancing traffic flow, and promoting safe driving. IoV communi-
cation can be broadly divided into intra-vehicle and inter-vehicle communication.
Intra-vehicle communication refers to data exchange within a vehicle through its mul-
tiple sensors and ECUs. This implies that engine performance, braking, and activation of 
airbags are constantly monitored and controlled. It enables seamless data transmission 
within a car, making it safer, more efficient, and more functional.
However, inter-vehicle communications are defined as communications between vari-
ous vehicles and other units connected within the network. These are classified into four 
major divisions: Vehicle-to-Pedestrian (V2P), Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V), Vehicle-to-
Infrastructure (V2I), and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G). V2V creates an environment where

Intra‑vehicle communication
Intra-vehicle connections rely on serial communication standards to facilitate message 
exchange between ECUs and various in-vehicle sensors. Table 2 compares three domi-
nant network protocols for intra-vehicle networks in terms of standard, domain, applica-
tion, and bit rate.
CAN is a standard serial automotive communication interface. Two channels, Low-
Speed CAN (LS) and High-Speed CAN (HS), are part of the conventional CAN bus 
structure. LS CAN functions within a data rate range of 40 Kbps to 250 Kbps, whereas 
HS CAN can accommodate a data rate of up to 1 Mbps. ECUs follow the rule of using 
one of the two protocols depending on the importance. All nodes within a car’s network 
can join the bus randomly, and data dissemination utilizes the CAN protocol with a dis-
semination protocol. Between urgent messages and priority requirements, priorities are 
also managed by a mechanism of arbitration. HS CAN is, therefore, generally employed 
by ECUs and sensors to perform safety-sensitive operations. In contrast, non-urgent or 
less time-sensitive nodes may take advantage of LS CAN. The adoption of CAN within 
contemporary automobiles can be attributed to its cost-effectiveness, simplicity of 
implementation, and minimal communication overhead.
FlexRay is a new standard for intra-vehicle communication that was co-developed 
by automotive leaders, including BMW, Philips, Freescale, and Bosch. FlexRay uses 
two independent communication buses. FlexRay offers several advantages over CAN,

Inter‑vehicle communication
While sensor limitations restrict data acquisition and accuracy, inter-vehicle commu-
nication can improve driver efficiency by leveraging statistics collected from nearby 
vehicles or a shared infrastructure. As outlined in Table 3, numerous communication 
standards have been proposed for inter-vehicle communication. These protocols deliver 
superior safety features, timely traffic management, and collaborative driving.
Dedicated Short-Range Communication (DSRC) is a wireless communication stand-
ard derived from the IEEE 802.11p protocol, an adaptation of the IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi 
standard specifically designed for use in automotive environments. It is designed to 
facilitate low-latency, high-efficiency, and fault-free communication, and is thus ideally 
deployed on V2V and V2I links. DSRC’s communication system architecture, derived 
from European standards and based on the specifications of the CAR-2-CAR Communi-
cation Consortium, consists of three main entities: the Roadside Unit (RSU), the Appli-
cation Unit (AU), and the On-Board Unit (OBU). DSRC’s structure and corresponding 
standards are shown in Fig. 2.
The OBU is an on-board communication unit that interacts with roadside infrastruc-
ture and other vehicles in its vicinity. The OBUs, which are integrated with IEEE 802.11p 
radios, serve as mobile terminals for short-range communication of high-speed infor-
mation, supporting cooperative driving, safety services, and autonomous driving. An 
OBU can be connected to multiple AUs and relay information from other OBUs on the 
network.
RSU is an abbreviation for a fixed roadside unit, a communication node for V2I com-
munication. It is utilized for local infrastructure access to exchange safety–critical and 
service-related information between vehicles and the entire communication network. 
Often incorporated with other network equipment, RSUs are applied to access backhaul 
networks or cloud servers for enhanced traffic control and city mobility services.

In addition to the physical components, the DSRC communication stack comprises 
multiple protocol layers. The physical (PHY) layer, based on IEEE 1609.4, manages the 
wireless transmission of signals. Above it, the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer 
includes the IEEE 802.11p standard for channel access and the IEEE 1609.4 MAC sub-
layer for channel coordination and multi-channel operation. The network layer uti-
lizes traditional Internet protocols, including TCP and UDP, for packet delivery. The 
service layer incorporates the IEEE 1609.3 WAVE Short Message Protocol (WSMP), 
which supports the efficient exchange of time-sensitive information between nodes. 
At the top, the application layer is divided into safety applications (e.g., collision 
avoidance, emergency braking alerts) and non-safety applications (e.g., infotainment, 
navigation assistance). Protection against malicious attacks is provided through IEEE 
1609.2 security services, which include data authentication, message integrity, and 
privacy protection, covering all levels.
Digital twin technology in IoV
Definition
DT was introduced by Michael Grieves in the early  2000 s and evolved into a ground-
breaking concept driven by digitized advances. Although a clear definition is lacking 
in the academic literature, various interpretations have been proposed, as summa-
rized in Table 4.
Recent breakthroughs in data processing techniques, including pattern recogni-
tion, extensive data analysis, and Artificial Intelligence (AI), have facilitated the tran-
sition of DTs from theoretical constructs to practical applications [18]. A pivotal 
moment occurred in 2011 when an article on DTs outlined their potential for predict-
ing the structural life of aircraft. This significantly departed from the conventional

DT technology enables the end-to-end integration of physical and virtual environ-

Modeling and simulation
The realization of efficient DT necessitates the modeling and simulation of data transfer. 
Virtual representation and its relationship with physical entities are used to define mod-
els to represent real objects. Five core elements are generally involved in this process: 
physical modeling, virtual modeling, data modeling, connection, and service.
•	 Physical modelling: in this step, the entity’s structure, characteristics, and working 
parameters are specified. Examples of IoV specifications include engine parts, body 
frames, sensors, and mechanical components.
•	 Virtual modeling: Physical entities are digitally represented through virtual modeling. 
It is a method of creating a virtual model based on the attributes and behavior of a 
physical entity, utilizing software tools. As the core of DT, the virtual model facili-
tates simulation and simulated experimentation.
•	 Data modelling is necessary to provide the DT with a real-time representation of 
what is happening. It dictates how data from the physical world gets captured, pro-
cessed, and translated into a virtual model. Proper data modelling empowers the DT 
to maintain a current and reliable representation of the physical object.
•	 Connection: physical and virtual models are linked through communication proto-
cols. This linkage permits the physical object and its DT to be synchronized at all

Development stages
Creating a DT requires several vital phases, each complemented by extensive data usage, 
from building models to integrating physical and virtual tools. The first phase of devel-
oping a DT involves creating a detailed model that represents the physical entity. This 
phase requires comprehensive data to accurately define the entity’s structure, charac-
teristics, and operating parameters. For example, in the IoV context, data from various 
sources, such as CAD models, material specifications, and sensor configurations, are 
crucial for creating a reliable virtual model of a vehicle.
It must then be integrated into current information from the physical system after 
the model is developed. It can be sensor data, environmental conditions, and operating 
parameters. Ongoing input of information ensures that the DT will always be a current 
and precise representation of the physical system, accommodating real-time control and 
monitoring. In IoV, it could involve constantly inputting information from on-board sen-
sors on a vehicle into its DT for current updates.
The DT can also conduct simulations for different scenarios, predict outcomes, and 
perform performance analysis under various conditions. The DT will also rely heavily 
on real-time and historical information to produce accurate simulations. For predictive 
maintenance for IoV, for example, significant historical vehicle performance and servic-
ing history record information will be required for analysis to identify likely failures and 
improve servicing schedules.
DT information identifies optimization inefficiencies and increases the efficiency of 
the physical system. Data-informed recommendations from the DT are used for better 
operations, maintenance, and resource allocation decisions. For an IoV application, such 
optimization would be used, for instance, to optimize traffic lights in real time based on 
vehicle and traffic infrastructure data to minimize traffic congestion and optimize traffic 
flows.
The final step consists of smoothly integrating virtual and physical systems to produce 
an operational DT that synchronizes its operations with its physical twin. The integra-
tion involves constantly sharing and processing information to facilitate synchroniz-
ing and real-time communication. In IoV, integrating digital vehicle twins into traffic 
infrastructure facilitates responding to changing road conditions in real time, thereby 
improving traffic efficiency and safety.
Role of DT in IoV
DT technology also features IoV environments through real-time surveillance, dynamic 
analysis, and predictive optimization of infrastructure and vehicle systems. By creating

permanently synchronized virtual replicas, DTs enhance system coordination, opti-
mize traffic control, and enable active maintenance policies, thereby contributing to 
higher transportation network safety and efficiency. There are two ways in which DTs 
can be adopted in IoV: DTs for individual vehicles and DTs for large-scale transport sys-

The first method relies on incorporating DT technology into individual automobiles. 
In this case, each automobile would have an onboard DT that mimics its operational and 
physical characteristics virtually. The DT is also constantly supplied with new data from 
its sensor suite, on-board units, and other sources, and it can precisely indicate the vehi-
cle’s current state and behavior.
The operational framework of single-vehicle DTs is essentially based on the network 
model of in-vehicle networks. While the primary communication method is still bus-
based, wireless communication is complementary. This framework’s simulation objects 
include drivers and vehicles, two key components of driving simulation.
Various sensors, including radars, inertial navigation systems, temperature sensors, 
mechanical sensors, and individual ECU modules, primarily collect real-time vehicle 
parameters. This data is then transferred to a data bus. On-board servers synchronize 
data from each node to manage the virtual twin. Three main channels transmit driver 
data to the IoV: driving records (creating driving behavior models), sensor readings (col-
lecting real-time physical indicators), and mobile device access (providing current health 
status information).
On-board servers report analysis results to the user’s in-vehicle terminals or mobile 
devices via wireless networks or data buses. The application layer displays these results 
in a user-friendly manner. Figure 3 illustrates how virtual and physical elements operate 
at varying scales within the system, with their communication and behavior being coor-
dinated. In terms of user experience, virtual and physical spaces are virtually equivalent, 
with the communications layer seamlessly bridging the heterogeneity of channels and 
connections.

DT technology holds enormous potential for enhancing the effectiveness and effi-

The perception layer sits at the bottom of the architecture, where ground transport

received and collected to maintain an accurate and up-to-date digital copy of the trans-
port infrastructure.
Operating between the perception and higher layers, the network layer securely and 
reliably conveys harvested information to higher layers. It utilizes communication tech-
nologies such as V2V, V2I, DSRC, and 5G networks to facilitate the seamless exchange of 
information between vehicles, infrastructure, and cloud servers. The layer provides the

Edge computing in IoV
The IoV comprises an integrated network of vehicles, infrastructure, and devices 
requiring efficient communication and information processing. Due to the exponen-
tial generation of information from such integrated elements, traditional central-
ized cloud computing faces challenges such as increased latency, network traffic, and 
reduced real-time responsiveness [33]. To address such challenges, edge computing 
has been recognized as a significant technology within the IoV infrastructure, which 
decentralizes information processing close to its point of generation. Table  5 illus-
trates how edge computing addresses these challenges and provides key advantages, 
including reduced latency, optimized bandwidth, enhanced security, real-time pro-
cessing, scalability, and resilience factors, all of which are crucial for the efficient and 
reliable execution of IoV solutions.
Edge computing is a distributed computing approach in which data handling, stor-
age, and computation occur at or near the data source rather than relying entirely 
on a centralized cloud server. In the context of IoV, edge computing involves placing 
computing resources, such as servers and smart devices, at the network’s edge, close 
to vehicles, road units, and other infrastructure components. This proximity to the 
data source results in faster processing, lower response times, and improved perfor-
mance, which are essential for real-time IoV applications.
Low latency is a key strength of edge computing. In IoV applications, real-time 
decision-making is a requirement, as seen in autonomous vehicles, intelligent traf-
fic lights, and collision avoidance systems; even milliseconds can become a turning 
point. With data processed locally at the edge, vehicles and infrastructure can quickly 
adapt to changing scenarios, thereby improving efficiency and safety.
Edge computing reduces the need to send bulk information to central cloud serv-
ers, safeguarding network bandwidth. In an IoV infrastructure where multiple gadgets 
generate vast amounts of information, edge computing helps to process and sort this

Processing at the edge can increase the privacy and security of IoV networks. In 
the case of highly sensitive data, such as driving habits or vehicle location data, pro-
cessing can occur locally at the edge. It would never be transmitted over long dis-
tances to central servers, reducing the possibility of compromise and exploitation. 
Security can also be enforced closer where information is generated using edge com-
puting, providing an additional level of protection.
The ability to perform real-time analysis and decision-making at the edge also 
ranks among the most significant advantages of edge computing for IoV. For exam-
ple, an autonomous vehicle can be equipped with an edge computing device that 
performs real-time analysis of sensor data to avoid obstacles, navigate, and ensure 
road safety. In a similar vein, traffic control can be designed to analyze informa-
tion from multiple sources in real-time and control traffic for optimal efficiency and 
minimal congestion.
Edge computing also supports scalability because it can split computing between 
multiple edge nodes. This decentralizing aspect makes IoV systems easier to scale

and devices into clusters. These clusters are managed together, allowing more efficient 
resource allocation, data processing, and communication. Clustering reduces the com-

ageable groups. This section covers various clustering algorithms and their applications

Hierarchical clustering is an algorithmic way of clustering devices into a multi-level, 
tree-like structure. In this approach, devices are grouped at different levels of the hier-

cles can further be grouped based on regional proximity, thereby building a hierarchy of 
the entire network.
Hierarchical clustering ensures efficient data aggregation by processing data at multi-
ple levels of the hierarchy before being transferred to the central server or higher-level 
nodes. This reduces the amount of data sent over long distances, saves bandwidth, and 
lowers latency. The multi-level properties of hierarchical clustering enable it to be highly 
scalable, as one can insert new devices into an existing hierarchy without disrupting the 
entire setup. Hierarchical clustering is scalable, considering different scales of opera-
tions, and can easily serve small and large networks of IoV.

Matching algorithms
In the IoV, matching algorithms play a crucial role in resource allocation by matching 
the requirements of vehicles and devices with the available resources within the net-
work. Effective matching ensures that computing power, bandwidth, storage, and other 
resources are used optimally, improving network efficiency and performance. This sec-
tion examines various matching techniques commonly used in IoV, with a focus on 
bipartite and market-based matching approaches.
Bipartite matching is a matching algorithm that creates a bipartite graph, where two 
sets of nodes represent the entities to be matched. In the IoV context, one set of nodes 
may represent vehicles or devices that require resources. In contrast, the other nodes 
represent the available resources, such as edge servers or network bandwidth. The goal 
of bipartite matching is to find the optimal match between these two sets, ensuring that 
each vehicle or device is paired with the most suitable resource.
Bipartite matching ensures resources are utilized accordingly to achieve maximum 
network-wide efficiency. By selectively matching vehicles with edge servers depending 
on their distances, available resources, and the demands of their respective tasks, this 
approach reduces latency and enhances load balancing. Load balancing, in particular, is 
something this algorithm excels at by distributing load across numerous edge servers, 
preventing one server from being overwhelmed while others remain idle. This makes for 
more stable and efficient network performance. Bipartite matching scales well with net-
work size and can be effectively applied even in large-scale IoV systems with numerous 
vehicles and resources.
Bipartite matching pairs vehicles with edge servers in real time and routes computing 
tasks to offload on optimal servers based on network status. The strategy can also bal-
ance network resources, such as bandwidth, by matching vehicles with high data com-
munication needs to network sections with corresponding capability.
Market-oriented matching mechanisms view resources within the IoV network as 
tradable commodities within a market environment. In this mechanism design, vehicles 
or devices requiring resources behave as buyers, whereas resource providers (network

This ensures that edge resources are allocated to the vehicles that need them most while 
maximizing revenue for service providers.
Stable matching algorithms, such as the Gale-Shapley algorithm, aim to find a stable 
pairing between two sets of entities where no pair would prefer a different match over 
the current one. In IoV, robust matching ensures that vehicles and resources are paired 
in a mutually satisfactory manner, thereby reducing the likelihood of disruptions or 
inefficiencies.
Stable matching algorithms ensure that vehicles and resources are paired fairly, reduc-
ing the likelihood of resource monopolization by specific vehicles or devices. The match-
ing stability ensures that neither party is incentivized to pursue a different pairing after a 
match, resulting in more consistent and predictable network operations.
When multiple stakeholders (e.g., different vehicle manufacturers or service providers) 
share resources, stable matching ensures that resources are allocated acceptably to eve-
ryone involved. Stable matching enables vehicles to be matched with edge servers based 
on predefined service level agreements, ensuring that both parties are satisfied with the 
resource allocation conditions.
Auction-based matching is another market-driven approach that allocates resources 
based on competitive bidding processes. Vehicles or devices bid for resources allocated 
to the highest bidder. For resource providers, auction-based matching can be a lucrative 
resource allocation method as it allows them to capitalize on the high demand for scarce 
resources. Auction-based matching ensures that resources are allocated to those who 
value them the most, as reflected in their bids. This leads to efficient use of resources, 
especially in environments where demand exceeds supply.
In an IoV network, edge servers could auction their computing resources to vehicles 
that need computing power. Vehicles with critical tasks can bid higher to secure the nec-
essary resources. Auction-based matching can also allocate radio spectrum to ensure 
that vehicles requiring high bandwidth for data-intensive tasks can secure the essential 
spectrum through tenders.

Offloading strategies
Offloading strategies are crucial to resource management in the IoV. These strategies 
involve transferring computing tasks from vehicles with limited computing power and 
energy resources to more powerful edge servers or cloud servers. Offloading can sig-
nificantly enhance the performance of IoV applications by reducing the computing load 
on vehicles, conserving energy, and accelerating task execution. This section examines 
various offloading strategies, focusing on partial offloading, full offloading, and hybrid 
approaches.
Partial offloading is a strategy that splits computing tasks between the vehicle and 
the edge server. The decision about which parts of the task to outsource is typically 
based on resource availability, task complexity, network conditions, and latency 
requirements. Partial outsourcing makes sense when specific tasks can be processed 
efficiently on the vehicle, while more resource-intensive components are better suited 
to the edge server.
By processing time-critical tasks locally in the vehicle, partial offloading can reduce 
latency and ensure that critical decisions, such as those required for autonomous 
driving, can be made without delay. Partial outsourcing allows for a more flexible 
utilization of available resources. Vehicles can perform more straightforward tasks 
locally, reducing the need for continuous data transmission and saving bandwidth. 
Partial discharge can help control vehicle energy consumption by discharging only 
the most resource-intensive parts of a task, allowing the vehicle to save energy for 
other functions.
For autonomous vehicles, partial offloading can process sensor data locally for 
immediate decisions (e.g., obstacle detection). In contrast, more complex data analy-
sis (e.g., route optimization) can be offloaded to an edge server. Vehicles can process 
basic navigation tasks locally while offloading more complex traffic pattern analysis 
and predictions to the edge.
With full offloading, complete computing tasks are transferred from the vehicle to 
an edge server or cloud server. This strategy is particularly beneficial for vehicles with 
limited computing power, such as older models or low-cost vehicles, which may not 
have the necessary hardware to perform complex calculations.
This paradigm enables centralized data processing where edge servers can aggregate 
data from multiple vehicles, resulting in richer analytics and insights. By outsourcing 
all computing tasks, vehicles can be designed with simpler and more cost-effective 
on-board systems, thereby reducing manufacturing costs and energy consumption. 
Full offloading uses the total computing power of edge servers, which are typically 
much more potent than vehicle-on-board systems. This allows complex tasks that 
would be impossible or inefficient to execute locally.
Full offloading is ideal for applications requiring significant computing resources, 
such as creating high-resolution maps, complex ML algorithms for autonomous driv-
ing, or real-time video processing for surveillance. Electric vehicles, particularly those 
designed to extend battery life, can benefit from full discharge, as it minimizes the 
energy requirements of on-board computers.

such as network latency, server load, and vehicle computing capacity.
Combining partial and full offloading, hybrid strategies can maintain reliability even 
under fluctuating network conditions or resource limitations. Hybrid discharge offers 
the best of both worlds, allowing the system to dynamically select the most appropri-

performance regardless of fluctuations in network or system status. Hybrid offloading 
can optimize performance by leveraging local computation when network conditions 
are poor or latency is critical, and using full offloading when maximum computing 
power is required.
In advanced driver assistance systems, hybrid offloading can dynamically adapt the 
processing load to real-time needs. For example, in high-speed driving scenarios, the 
system could offload critical tasks to edge servers for rapid computation, while in less 
demanding situations, it could process tasks locally. Hybrid offloading can be used in 
innovative city environments where vehicles interact with various infrastructure ele-
ments (e.g., traffic lights and road sensors). Depending on the distance and latency, the 
system can process the data locally or offload it to nearby edge servers.
Opportunistic offloading exploits temporary opportunities to offload tasks when net-
work resources are temporarily underutilized or when the vehicle encounters a favorable 
situation, such as approaching an edge server. This approach relies on continuous envi-
ronmental monitoring to determine the optimal times and locations for discharge.
By outsourcing tasks only when conditions are optimal, opportunistic outsourcing can 
reduce the costs associated with data transfer and processing, particularly in scenarios 
where pricing models fluctuate in response to demand. Opportunistic offloading ensures 
that resources are utilized when they are most available, thereby reducing the strain on 
network and computing resources during peak times.
In scenarios where vehicles move through areas with varying network coverage and 
edge server availability, opportunistic offloading can ensure that tasks are offloaded 
when the vehicle is best positioned to do so. For in-vehicle entertainment systems that 
stream content, opportunistic offloading can adjust the quality of the stream or buffer 
content based on the availability of network resources.
With cooperative offloading, multiple vehicles work together to share the comput-

server serving the group, effectively creating a local processing cluster. Cooperative off-

compared to offloading to a remote cloud server. Through cooperative offloading, vehi-
cles can pool their resources to complete tasks that would be too demanding for a single 
vehicle to handle. If a vehicle in the cooperation network fails, others can take over its 
tasks, ensuring the continuity of service.

Security and privacy in digital twin‑enabled IoV systems
Integrating DT and IoV technologies presents unprecedented opportunities for real-
time monitoring, optimization, and predictive analysis in vehicular environments. 
Connectedness, however, gives rise to both security and privacy risks. Personal infor-
mation, including driver authentication, vehicle location, work status, and driving 
behavior, is continuously collected and transmitted over separate networks. A data 
breach can have severe implications, including loss of privacy, service disruptions, 
and potential bodily harm. Security and confidentiality protection are key in DT-ena-
bled IoV environments for achieving trust, reliability, and system resilience. To better 
understand the risks at stake, Table 8 provides an overview of the most significant 
security and privacy risks associated with DT-enabled IoV environments.
Several high-profile incidents have demonstrated that vehicles and transporta-
tion infrastructure are highly vulnerable to cyberattacks. For instance, hijacking DTs 
could allow attackers to send malicious commands to vehicles, tamper with predic-
tive maintenance schedules, or disrupt traffic management systems. To mitigate these 
challenges, a range of countermeasures has been proposed. Table 9 summarizes the 
prominent solutions for enhancing security and privacy in DT-enabled IoV systems.
End-to-end encryption, such as Transport Layer Security (TLS), can safeguard V2I 
communications against MITM attacks. Lightweight cryptography must also be used 
for an automotive system with limited resources to provide decent security and mini-
mal computational overhead. Blockchain-based identity management can be applied 
to give tamper-resistant authentication to infrastructure nodes, vehicles, and digital 
twins. It can be used to preserve trust for even very large-scale dynamic IoV networks.
Secure computation offloading ensures that computations offloaded to cloud or edge 
servers are safe and utilizes mechanisms such as homomorphic encryption, trusted 
execution environments, and zero-knowledge proofs. Intrusion detection mechanisms, 
such as machine learning-based intrusion detection systems, can identify abnormal 
behavior in real time, including unauthorized resource usage, abnormal traffic, or unu-
sual vehicle behavior [73].
Privacy-preserving data aggregation allows various vehicles to share information with-
out revealing individual and detailed operational information. Data and user privacy are 
preserved through mechanisms such as federated learning, ensuring that local data and 
user privacy are maintained while global-level models are obtained. Trust management 
mechanisms adaptively consider network components and vehicle trust, thereby reduc-
ing the potential for insider attacks and compromised nodes.
In addition to classical blockchains, Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT) offer 
decentralized, tamper-proof mechanisms for securely sharing information. Transpar-
ency, accountability, and auditing are provided through event and transaction record-
ing on multiple nodes by DLT, without single points of failure, making unauthorized 
information tampering exceedingly unlikely. Lightweight cryptography reduces the 
computational requirements of cryptographic operations for resource-constrained envi-
ronments, such as those found in vehicles and edge nodes. These operations ensure

Future research directions
With the advancement of integrating DT technology with edge computing for IoV, 
various research directions have arisen, primarily from a resource management view-
point. As outlined in Table 10, these directions aim to address the scalability, effec-
tiveness, security, and flexibility issues of DT-enabled IoV systems.
Future work is crucial for developing adaptively adjusting resource control algo-
rithms that dynamically respond to ever-changing IoV network conditions. Those 
algorithms must consider changing flow rates, varying car densities, and volatile envi-
ronmental conditions. Using real-time information from DTs, such algorithms have 
the potential to continuously realign resources for optimal performance while mini-
mizing latency within the network. Studies can use ML and AI to forecast demand 
and optimize resource utilization in real-time.
Today’s resource management methods are generally implemented within individual 
layers, specifically the network, computing, and storage layers. Such resources must 
be managed across multiple levels simultaneously under a cross-layer resource man-
agement methodology. It can be researched how DTs can be incorporated into such a 
cross-layer methodology to enable a higher level of resource management. This involves 
developing frameworks for seamless communication and coordination at various levels 
to efficiently coordinate resources within the IoV environment.
Scalability improves with the expansion of IoV networks. Future work should focus 
on designing scalable resource management systems to handle an increasing number of 
vehicular and device connections. It can be done by looking into decentralized manage-
ment of resources using edge computing and DTs for distributing computing burdens 
over numerous nodes. It can also examine hierarchical clustering and other scalable 
algorithms for the efficient and effective management of resources at an IoV network 
scale.
Cooperative DTs, where multiple DTs for various vehicles or parts of the infrastruc-
ture collaborate, present new challenges and new resource management opportunities. 
Future research can explore ways of managing resources so that multiple DTs can collab-

Conclusions
DT technology, combined with edge computing, represents a transformative advance-
ment for the IoV and offers significant potential to enhance the efficiency, safety, and 
reliability of connected vehicle systems. This survey examined the different resource 
management approaches in DT-enabled edge computing, focusing on clustering, 
matching algorithms, and offloading strategies. Each method is responsible for opti-
mizing computing, network, and storage assets to meet the advanced and dynamic 
requirements of IoV applications. The debate centered on how clustering techniques 
address extensive networks by grouping vehicles and devices, enabling efficient data 
collection and communication. Matching algorithms, on the other hand, ensure that 
resources are optimally allocated by coupling demand with available resources. At the 
same time, offloading strategies distribute computing tasks between vehicles and edge 
servers, improving overall system performance and energy efficiency. Future direc-
tions for developing resource management for DT-based IoV systems have been pre-
sented. They include the development of adaptive resource management algorithms, 
cross-layer designs, scalable mechanisms for large-scale IoV networks, and AI and 
machine learning integration for predictive management. Overcoming complexities 
related to security, privacy, and standardization issues will enable the widespread 
adoption and success of the IoV.

Abstract: The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) enables advanced developments in automotive systems to communicate with interconnected devices, enhancing traffic flow, security, and util- ity functions. Edge computing and Digital Twins (DTs) facilitate effective resource management in the IoV. DTs replicate real entities in the virtual domain with real-time control, diagnostics, maintenance, and better management. With edge computing, processing data near the source, these technologies significantly lower response time and optimize system performance. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the latest resource management strategies in DT-enabled edge computing for IoV. Existing approaches are then discussed and compared using clustering, matching, and offloading approaches. Clustering groups of vehicles and devices to manage resources while assigning resources by mapping demand and availability. Offload- ing techniques delegate computation to edge servers, thereby controlling resources. The paper outlines the strengths and weaknesses of each method, as well as research directions, including the integration of artificial intelligence, security and privacy issues, and interoperability standards.
